newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ may help support Thai baht, but not yet - dealers.
newsitem.headline: BOJ may help support Thai baht, but not yet - dealers.

text.p: Japan's central bank said on Thursday it may join hands with other Asian central banks and intervene in foreign exchange markets to help support the crumbling Thai baht if asked to do so by Thailand.
Any such moves would be part of the Asian currency safety net agreement reached between Asian monetary authorities in 1996, an official at the Bank of Japan (BOJ) told Reuters.
"The agreement is there, although it is not a thing we would activate unless we were asked by Thailand," he said.
"We have an agreement, and if we want to use it, we certainly will. But it's not a question of our making the first move," he added.

Last year, Japan agreed with the monetary authorities of Australia, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand to establish bilateral repurchase agreements to provide liquidity in times of currency crisis.

Such "repo" pacts give participants instant access to cash -- for use to defend their currencies against excessive volatility -- by virtue of them selling their holdings in U.S. government securities to partners with a promise to buy them back later.
On Wednesday, in the first use of this agreement, the Thai central bank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore jointly intervened in the foreign exchange market to defend the baht.
Malaysia's central bank and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority were also said to have bought the Thai currency after it fell to 26.250-26.300 to the dollar, though there was no confirmation.

Rising concerns about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of political turmoil in the cabinet that could lead to the possible resignation of Thai Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan triggered heavy baht sales for the dollar on Wednesday.
Amnuay, who has repeatedly denied he will quit, reiterated on Thursday that Thailand will defend its currency against attacks in the market by currency speculators.
"We have been successful and we will be successful," he said, adding: "We have support from all our friends."

But Tokyo dealers said it may well take time before the BOJ joins any future moves, saying the Japanese central bank's main concern at this point is the dollar's volatile moves against the yen. The greenback has plunged more than 10 yen in the past two weeks, and some fear even more slides lie ahead.

"Right now the BOJ has its hands completely full just trying to deal with the dollar and yen. This isn't the time for it to think about other things," said one Asian currency dealer at a major Japanese bank.
He said, and others agreed, that if the Japanese central bank did agree to take part in joint intervention, the impact definitely would be stronger.

"But they would have to be very careful how they did it because to see the BOJ selling dollars, even against an Asian currency, risks sending a strange signal to the market and could accelerate the dollar's fall against the yen," he added.
A dealer with a long-term credit bank, citing the weak Thai economy, said he was concerned by the possibility that not all of Wednesday's sales were speculative.

"There's the worry that the flow of capital out of the country may be starting to pick up speed, meaning the weak currency situation could drag on for a long time and diminish the impact of any intervention," he said.

But most dealers said they felt it was unlikely the BOJ would refrain from taking part in future joint moves should the baht depreciate seriously, owing to the need to maintain favourable ties among other Asian nations and its huge financial involvement in the region.

"Totally aside from the question of its investment in Thailand, which of course is one concern, Japan has made a big deal about its cooperative ties with other Asian nations. So if the baht falls further, and the Bank of Thailand asks it to intervene, they will most likely take part," the credit-bank dealer said.
